newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian wage case offers inflation clue.
newsitem.headline: Australian wage case offers inflation clue.

text.p: Australia's Industrial Relations Commission is expected to rule before the end of March on a major wage claim which financial markets expect to deliver a clue into the direction of inflation.

A spokesman for Australia's chief union body, the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU), told Reuters that the ruling would set the minimum amount of pay workers could expect to receive over the next three years.

The government and the central bank, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), have said the size of the wage increases could have a marked effect on Australia's ability to hold inflation at its current low levels.
Earlier this month, RBA governor Ian Macfarlane said the bank was watching wages data closely for an indication of what would happen with inflation over the longer term.
As such, wage outcomes would also be considered as a significant part of any future monetary policy decisions that the bank made.

"If you have some important information on this (wages), either from the market sector or the administered sector (the commission), then it would be only logical to wait until you saw what the results were," Macfarlane said.
Australian wages must comply with certain minimum contracts -- "awards" -- which are set by the commission.
Workers can negotiate larger rises privately with their employers but, occasionally, awards for low-income earners are given a "safety net" adjustment to help people unable to negotiate a rise.
The government is proposing the tribunal grant such a safety net adjustment, raising the low-pay awards by A$8 (US$6) a week each year for the next three years.
But the ACTU wants much more. It is seeking an immediate rise of 8.75 percent plus A$20 a week for all awards, then two further A$20 rises in the next two years.
"If you don't have a boss that will give you a pay rise and you don't have an enterprise agreement, then this is the only way you'll get an increase," the ACTU spokesman said.
"So we don't want to be in a situation where award rates decline by such a great extent that they're completely irrelevant."

The government and the RBA have often warned the ACTU's claim, if approved, would threaten the country's low inflation rate, which was 2.1 percent for the year to the December quarter after large irregular items were excluded.
The government has also said it would probably lead to the loss of about 400,000 jobs.
"In the current economic environment, the ACTU's claim is simply irresponsible," Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith said in December.

"On the other hand, the government's position of an A$8 per week increase in each of the next three years protects the real value of wages of those on the lowest award classifications and more importantly, doesn't put their jobs at risk."

The coalition government, elected in March 1996 after 13 years of a Labor Party administration, has passed legislation to cut labour market regulation and to lessen the role of unions in wage negotiations.
